overview: This file documents disputes over press freedom, news gathering, and propaganda in East Asia during the Manchurian crisis. Its materials cover Chinese restrictions on Japanese newspapers and correspondents, the creation in Shanghai of a Japanese-sponsored Press Union to circulate its version of events, the reported capture of Japanese newspapermen, and Japanese news-agency stories alleging extensive American military assistance to China. State Department officials compared those stories with official export figures, judged them exaggerated or unfounded, and debated whether to raise the matter informally with Japanese Ambassador Katsuji Debuchi.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference concerning oppression of Japanese newspapers in China
subfiles.about: The sheet redirects readers to Forbes’s report on Chinese interference with Japanese newspapers and proposed Japanese diplomatic negotiations.
subfiles.summary: The filing note cross-references document no. 216 in file 894.00 P.R/41. It identifies the subject as the oppression of Japanese newspapers in China and records that the Japanese Legation had been instructed to negotiate a settlement.

subfiles.title: Discussion of Japanese newspapers in China
subfiles.about: A summary describes Japanese complaints about Chinese interference with newspapers, correspondents, and communications.
subfiles.summary: Japanese newspapers and correspondents protested attacks, seizures, mailing bans, and restrictions on telegraph and telephone use, while Chinese authorities attributed their actions to unfair Japanese interpretations of events. The dispute intensified after an attack on the Nanjing office of the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shimbun and the wounding of Asahi Shimbun correspondent Kusazo Chihara. Japanese newspaper representatives protested to the Chinese Minister in Tokyo on April 18.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference for Cunningham’s Press Union despatch
subfiles.about: The sheet redirects readers to despatch no. 7982 concerning a Press Union circular explaining the organization and its purposes.
subfiles.summary: This filing note cross-references despatch no. 7982 to file 793.94/3268. It identifies Cunningham at Shanghai as the sender and describes the subject as a circular issued by the Press Union.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 7982 forwarding material on the Press Union
subfiles.from: Edwin S. Cunningham, American Consul General at Shanghai
subfiles.about: Cunningham forwards a copy of his despatch to the American Legation concerning the Press Union Bulletin.
subfiles.summary: Cunningham encloses a copy of Shanghai Consulate General despatch no. 7063, together with its enclosure, for the Secretary of State. The forwarded material concerns the newly organized Press Union and its bulletin.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 7063 on the Press Union Bulletin
subfiles.from: Edwin S. Cunningham, American Consul General at Shanghai
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Minister at Beijing
subfiles.about: Cunningham reports on an October 8 circular announcing a Japanese-sponsored press service in Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: The circular claimed that unfounded or exaggerated rumors following the Manchurian incident had created a disturbing atmosphere and presented the new service as an effort to restore truth and facts. It openly described the Press Union as a Japanese intelligence organ sponsored by Japanese residents’ bodies, commercial and industrial associations, pressmen, and other members of Shanghai’s Japanese community. The despatch encloses a copy of the mimeographed October 8 letter; part of the final paragraph is badly corrupted in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference concerning captured Japanese newspapermen
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a report about Japanese newspapermen allegedly captured by Chinese forces and an effort to obtain their release.
subfiles.summary: The filing note cross-references document no. 71, also numbered no. 116 to the Legation, in file 894.20293/15. It reports that four Japanese newspapermen had allegedly been captured by the Chinese and that John N. Heijbroek was said to be undertaking a secret mission for Japanese authorities to secure their release.

subfiles.title: Hamilton memorandum on approaching Ambassador Debuchi
subfiles.about: Hamilton questions whether the State Department should raise Japanese news-agency misinformation with Ambassador Debuchi.
subfiles.summary: After seeing the attached memorandum in final form, Hamilton doubts the advisability of discussing its subject with Ambassador Debuchi. If the matter is mentioned, he recommends that Hornbeck do so only casually and informally. Page 9 contains a largely illegible handwritten routing or annotation note associated with the memorandum.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on misinformation issued by Japanese news agencies in China
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum evaluates Japanese reports alleging extensive American arms sales, aviation assistance, and financial support for China.
subfiles.summary: Drawing on telegrams from Beijing, the memorandum warns that Japanese information services were circulating reports that could revive anti-American feeling, including claims of major Chinese purchases of American aircraft and antiaircraft guns, the employment of American military specialists, a $15 million loan, and promised U.S. access to Chinese air bases. State Department information showed only thirteen privately employed American aviation advisers and substantially smaller arms exports: $391,155 to China during the first ten months of 1932, including twenty-two airplanes, compared with $270,509 to Japan. The Department therefore considered the reports exaggerated or implausible and noted that American regulations actually restricted arms sales to China but not to Japan. It suggested giving Ambassador Debuchi corrective information informally while withholding the precise number and value of aircraft exported to China.

interest: The file is useful for tracing how conflicts over reporting, censorship, and propaganda became part of the wider Manchurian crisis. Particularly revealing are the Press Union’s candid description of itself as a Japanese intelligence organ, the State Department’s use of detailed trade statistics to test sensational news reports, and its concern that even demonstrably implausible stories might revive anti-American sentiment. The cross-reference sheets also show how related evidence was dispersed across the State Department’s decimal filing system, while Hamilton’s later note exposes internal hesitation over whether correcting the record through Ambassador Debuchi would be diplomatically prudent.
